note.title: Concentration of solutions and atom economy
note.subject: science

given: Relative atomic masses from the Periodic Table on the Chemistry Data Leaflet
mustKnow: Concentration (mol/dm³) = moles ÷ volume (dm³), and its rearrangements
Atom economy = (mass of desired product ÷ total mass of products) × 100

notOnThisSpec: Concentration in g/dm³ as a required answer

mustBeAbleTo: Convert a volume in cm³ to dm³ by dividing by 1000, as the first line of working
Calculate a concentration in mol/dm³ from a mass of solute and a volume of solution
Calculate the moles of solute in a volume of solution of known concentration
Calculate the mass of solute needed for a given volume and concentration, with the Mr from the Data Leaflet
Calculate an atom economy from a balanced equation, multiplying each formula mass by its balancing number
Explain why a high atom economy matters for sustainable development and for economic reasons
Tell atom economy apart from percentage yield
sheet.howExamined: C2 Higher only: 1 hour 15 minutes, 80 marks, calculator and Chemistry Data Leaflet allowed. Concentration and atom economy often share one quantitative question. A mass-of-solute or concentration calculation is [2] to [3], one mark for each line (moles, Mr, answer), and error carried forward means an early slip costs only its own line. An atom economy is [3]: the desired mass with its balancing number, the total mass of products, the percentage, sometimes set as 'show that'. A 'why is it (not) sustainable' or 'why is a high atom economy important' part is [1] to [2] and wants wasted atoms and cost.
traps: Leaving the volume in cm³, so the moles or the mass come out a thousand times too big (Summer 2025 C2 H Q5(a)(ii))
Explaining why a preparation is not sustainable with 'it uses less energy', which earns nothing (Summer 2025 C2 H Q5(b)(ii))
Leaving a bracket unmultiplied in an Mr, such as Mg(NO₃)₂ (Summer 2025 C1 H Q6(a))
Using one relative atomic mass where the formula has two atoms of that element (Summer 2025 C1 H Q6(b)(i))
Dropping a balancing number from the desired product or from the total mass of products
Turning the atom economy fraction upside down: an answer over 100% is always a sign
Giving a concentration in g/dm³ when mol/dm³ is asked
Confusing atom economy, which comes from the equation, with percentage yield, which comes from an experiment

workedExamples.stem:
5.85 g of sodium chloride, NaCl, is dissolved in water and the solution is made up to 250 cm³.
Calculate the solution's concentration in mol/dm³. [3]
Use the Data Leaflet for relative atomic masses.

steps.decision: Convert before anything else, on a line of its own. The formula divides by dm³, and this is the line where most lost marks begin.

steps.working: Mr of NaCl = 23 + 35.5 = 58.5, so moles = mass ÷ Mr = 5.85 ÷ 58.5 = 0.100 mol.
steps.decision: Concentration counts moles, so the grams have to become moles first, exactly as in C1. The relative atomic masses come from the Data Leaflet.

options: Because concentration in mol/dm³ counts moles, not grams
Because 58.5 is the volume of the solution
Because every concentration question gives the moles directly
whyMenu.explain: The unit gives it away: mol/dm³ is moles per cubic decimetre, so a mass must be turned into moles before it goes into the formula.

steps.decision: Moles on top, volume underneath. A quick sense check: a tenth of a mole in a quarter of a dm³ is four tenths of a mole in a whole one.

steps.working: Volume = 250 ÷ 1000 = 0.250 dm³, so moles = concentration × volume = 0.400 × 0.250 = 0.100 mol.
steps.decision: The concentration tells you the moles in each dm³, so multiply by how many dm³ there are. Convert the volume on the way.

options: Because moles = concentration × volume, and the volume must be in dm³
Because the 250 is already in dm³
whyMenu.explain: Concentration is moles per dm³, so moles = concentration × dm³. Dividing would give a number with no meaning here.

steps.decision: Three oxygens, so 16 is multiplied by 3. The Mr is a mark on its own, so show the sum.
Moles times Mr gives grams. Dividing instead gives a tiny number: a tenth of a mole of anything weighs more than a gram or two.

items.stem: What is the relative formula mass, Mr, of sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃? (Na = 23, C = 12, O = 16)
items.skill: Prerequisite from C1 §1.7: relative formula mass. You are not expected to have met this lesson yet.

options.feedback: 2 × 23 + 12 + 3 × 16 = 106. Every Mr in this lesson is built the same way, one subscript at a time.
That counts one sodium. The subscript 2 after Na doubles it: 2 × 23 = 46, so the Mr is 106.
That counts one of each atom. Each subscript multiplies the atom before it: two sodiums and three oxygens.

items.stem: How many moles are there in 20 g of sodium hydroxide, NaOH (Mr = 40)?
items.skill: Prerequisite from C1 §1.7: moles from a mass.

options.feedback: Moles = mass ÷ Mr = 20 ÷ 40 = 0.5. This lesson uses that line in almost every calculation.
That is Mr ÷ mass, the fraction upside down. Moles = mass ÷ Mr = 20 ÷ 40.
That multiplies the mass by the Mr. To go from grams to moles, divide by the Mr.

items.stem: What is the mass of 0.25 mol of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃ (Mr = 100)?
items.skill: Prerequisite from C1 §1.7: a mass from moles.

options.feedback: Mass = moles × Mr = 0.25 × 100 = 25 g.
That is Mr ÷ moles. From moles back to grams you multiply: 0.25 × 100.
That divides the moles by the Mr. Going from moles to grams, multiply by the Mr.

items.stem: What is the Mr of calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂? (Ca = 40, O = 16, H = 1)
items.skill: Prerequisite from C1 §1.7: a bracket in a formula.

options.feedback: 40 + 2 × (16 + 1) = 74. The 2 outside the bracket multiplies everything inside it.
That ignores the 2 outside the bracket. It doubles the whole OH group: 2 × 17 = 34.
Only the oxygen has been doubled. The 2 outside the bracket doubles the hydrogen as well.

items.stem: How many cm³ are there in 1 dm³?
items.skill: Know the conversion between cm³ and dm³

options.feedback: A cube 10 cm on each edge: 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000 cm³.
That would be a square 10 cm by 10 cm, which is an area. A volume has three dimensions: 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000.
A decimetre is 10 cm, but a cubic decimetre is 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000 cm³.

items.stem: Which of these gives a concentration in mol/dm³?

options.feedback: Moles per dm³: the unit spells out the formula.
That is the fraction upside down. Read the unit: mol/dm³ is moles divided by dm³.
Multiplying gives nothing useful here. Concentration is moles shared out per dm³, so divide.

options.text: mass in grams ÷ volume in dm³
options.feedback: That gives grams per dm³. CCEA's unit is mol/dm³, so turn the mass into moles first.

items.stem: 0.200 mol of solute is dissolved to make 500 cm³ of solution. What is the concentration?
items.skill: Calculate a concentration, converting the volume

options.feedback: That divides by 500, the volume in cm³. Convert first: 500 cm³ = 0.500 dm³.
That is volume ÷ moles. Concentration is moles ÷ volume: 0.200 ÷ 0.500.
That multiplies the moles by the volume. Concentration divides: 0.200 ÷ 0.500.

items.stem: How many moles of solute are there in 20.0 cm³ of a solution of concentration 0.500 mol/dm³?
items.skill: Calculate moles from a concentration and a volume

options.feedback: That multiplies by 20.0, the volume still in cm³. Convert first: 20.0 cm³ = 0.0200 dm³.
That divides the concentration by the volume. Moles = concentration × volume.
That divides the volume by the concentration. Moles = concentration × volume.

items.stem: Solution P holds 0.10 mol in 250 cm³. Solution Q holds 0.30 mol in 1.00 dm³. Which is more concentrated?

options.text: P, because each dm³ of it holds 0.40 mol
options.feedback: 0.10 ÷ 0.250 = 0.40 mol/dm³ for P, against 0.30 mol/dm³ for Q.

options.text: Q, because it contains more solute
options.feedback: Q holds more moles, but spread through four times the volume. Concentration is moles per dm³: P has 0.40, Q has 0.30.
0.10 ÷ 250 uses the volume in cm³. In dm³, P is 0.10 ÷ 0.250 = 0.40 mol/dm³, which beats Q's 0.30.

items.stem: Which expression gives the atom economy for making a product?

options.text: (mass of desired product ÷ total mass of products) × 100
options.feedback: The product you want, over everything the equation makes, as a percentage.

options.text: (total mass of products ÷ mass of desired product) × 100
options.feedback: Upside down: this always gives more than 100%, which is impossible for an atom economy.

options.text: (mass of desired product ÷ mass of by-products) × 100
options.feedback: The bottom line is every product, the desired one included, not the waste alone.
That is percentage yield, which needs an experiment. Atom economy comes from the balanced equation.

items.stem: Methane and steam make hydrogen: CH₄ + H₂O → CO + 3H₂. What is the atom economy for making hydrogen? (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
items.skill: Calculate an atom economy with a balancing number

options.feedback: 3 × 2 = 6 of hydrogen out of 34 in total: 6 ÷ 34 × 100 = 17.6%.
That uses one H₂ instead of three. The balancing number 3 is part of the mass: 3 × 2 = 6.
That puts the carbon monoxide on top. The question wants hydrogen, so hydrogen goes on top.
Over 100% means the fraction is upside down: desired mass on top, total underneath.

items.stem: Why is a high atom economy important for sustainable development?
items.skill: Give the reason the scheme credits

options.text: fewer raw materials are used up and less waste is made
options.feedback: Both halves of the sustainability reason. The economic reason, lower costs, is the other mark.
Summer 2025 examiners did not credit energy answers. Atom economy is about atoms: raw materials used and waste made.
Speed is rate, a different topic. Atom economy says nothing about how fast a reaction goes.

options.text: more product is collected at the end of the experiment
options.feedback: That describes a high percentage yield. Atom economy is fixed by the equation, before any experiment.

Calcium oxide is made by heating calcium carbonate:
$\ce{CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2}$
Calculate the atom economy for making calcium oxide.

context.setting: Two routes to the painkiller ibuprofen

parts.stem:
The painkiller ibuprofen was first made by a six-step route with an atom economy of about 40%. A newer three-step route has an atom economy of about 77%.
Explain what is meant by atom economy and how it is worked out, and explain why the newer route is better for sustainable development and for economic reasons.
This question also assesses the quality of your written communication, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist chemical terms used widely and accurately; organised with clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar good enough that the meaning is clear throughout.
Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist chemical vocabulary; organised with some clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; organisation may lack clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave the intended meaning unclear.

indicativeContent.point: atom economy compares the mass of the desired product with the total mass of all the products
it is worked out as (mass of desired product ÷ total mass of products) × 100
keyWords: total mass of all the products

indicativeContent.point: it is found from the balanced symbol equation, before any experiment is done
in the newer route more of the atoms in the reactants end up in the ibuprofen (77% against 40%)
the older route turns about 60% of the mass into by-products
fewer raw materials are used up, so resources last longer: better for sustainable development
less waste is made, so there is less to dispose of and less pollution
it is cheaper: less is spent on raw materials and on dealing with waste

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Start with the definition and the formula.
Then compare the two figures in words: what happens to the other 60% or 23% of the mass?
Finish with one sustainable-development reason and one economic reason. Energy is not one of them.
parts.workedSolution: Atom economy compares the mass of the desired product with the total mass of all the products, as a percentage: (mass of desired product ÷ total mass of products) × 100. It is worked out from the balanced symbol equation, so it is known before any experiment is done. In the newer route 77% of the mass ends up as ibuprofen, against about 40% in the older route, where about 60% of the mass becomes by-products. So the newer route uses fewer raw materials to make the same amount of ibuprofen, which conserves resources and is better for sustainable development, and it makes less waste, so there is less to dispose of and less pollution. It is also cheaper, because less money is spent on raw materials that end up as waste and on dealing with that waste.

commonErrors.feedback: This answer argues from energy alone. Summer 2025 examiners did not credit energy on a sustainability question: use the atom economy figures, the wasted mass, the raw materials and the cost.

findTheMistake.stem:
Orla is asked: 'Calculate the mass of copper(II) sulfate, CuSO₄, needed to make 200 cm³ of a solution of concentration 0.250 mol/dm³. [3]'
Her answer:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 multiplies by 200, the volume in cm³. The concentration is moles per dm³, so the volume must be in dm³ first: 200 cm³ = 0.200 dm³. Lines 2 and 3 are done properly, which is why the answer is exactly a thousand times too big: 8000 g is eight kilograms for a small flask. The Summer 2025 report found this calculation hard, with most marks earned through the working that followed.
findTheMistake.feedback: Two of the three marks: the Mr is right, and multiplying moles by Mr is the right method, so it is carried forward. Only the moles line is lost. The habit that fixes it: write the volume in dm³ on its own line before the formula, and ask whether the final mass is believable.

findTheMistake.stem:
Dáire is asked: 'Aluminium is extracted from aluminium oxide: 2Al₂O₃ → 4Al + 3O₂. Calculate the atom economy for making aluminium. Give your answer to one decimal place. [3]'
His answer:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 keeps the 4 in front of Al, which is exactly right. Line 2 then forgets the 3 in front of O₂: the equation makes three oxygen molecules, 3 × 32 = 96, so the total mass of products is 108 + 96 = 204. Line 3 is the right method on the wrong total. A check would have caught it: the reactants, 2 × 102 = 204, must weigh the same as the products.
findTheMistake.feedback: Two of the three marks: the desired mass is right and the final line follows correctly from the total. The total is the mark that goes. Multiply every formula mass by its balancing number, and compare your product total with the reactant total before you divide.

findTheMistake.stem:
Niamh is asked: 'Calculate the concentration of a solution made by dissolving 8.20 g of calcium nitrate, Ca(NO₃)₂, in water and making it up to 250 cm³. [3]'
Her answer:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The 2 outside the bracket multiplies everything inside it, so Ca(NO₃)₂ has two nitrogens and six oxygens: 40 + 2 × (14 + 48) = 164. Line 2 counted only one nitrate group. Everything after it is the right method carried forward from the wrong Mr. This is the bracket slip the Summer 2025 C1 report describes.
findTheMistake.feedback: Two of the three marks: the volume conversion and the final division are right and carried forward. Only the Mr is lost. When a formula has a bracket, work out the group inside first (14 + 48 = 62), then multiply it by the number outside.

prompts.prompt: Write the formula for concentration, with its units.
To change a volume in cm³ into dm³, you …
How do you find the moles of solute in a volume of solution of known concentration?
prompts.answer: Moles = concentration × volume, with the volume in dm³.

prompts.prompt: Give the three lines for finding the mass of solute needed to make a solution.
prompts.answer: Moles = concentration × volume in dm³. Mr from the Data Leaflet. Mass = moles × Mr.

prompts.prompt: Write the formula for atom economy.
prompts.answer: Atom economy = (mass of desired product ÷ total mass of products) × 100.

prompts.prompt: Give a sustainable-development reason and an economic reason for wanting a high atom economy.
prompts.answer: Sustainable development: fewer raw materials are used up and less waste is made. Economic: less money is spent on raw materials and on getting rid of waste.

prompts.prompt: Why does 'it uses less energy' earn nothing when you are asked why a preparation is not sustainable?
prompts.answer: Atom economy is about atoms, not energy: the marks are for raw materials used up, waste made and the cost of both.

prompts.prompt: What is the atom economy of a reaction that makes only one product, and why?
prompts.answer: 100%, because every atom of the reactants ends up in the desired product.

prompts.prompt: What is the difference between atom economy and percentage yield?
prompts.answer: Atom economy comes from the balanced equation: the mass of the desired product over the total mass of products. Percentage yield comes from an experiment: the actual mass made over the most that could be made.

prompts.prompt: What is the atom economy for making calcium oxide by heating calcium carbonate, CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂?
prompts.answer: 56%: calcium oxide is 56 out of a total product mass of 56 + 44 = 100.

prompts.prompt: Your atom economy comes out at 212%. What has gone wrong?
prompts.answer: The fraction is upside down: put the desired mass on top and the total mass of products underneath. An atom economy can never be more than 100%.

findings.asked: Calculate the mass of an acid needed to make 250 cm³ of solution of a stated concentration in mol/dm³.
findings.wentWrong: Candidates found it hard; most still picked up some marks because each line of their working was followed through.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Turned 250 cm³ into 0.250 dm³, multiplied by the concentration to get the moles, worked out the Mr from the Data Leaflet, and multiplied the moles by the Mr.
findings.rule: Three lines, each worth a mark: moles = concentration × volume in dm³; the Mr; mass = moles × Mr. Write all three so a slip costs one mark, not three.

findings.asked: Show that a laboratory preparation had a given atom economy from its balanced equation, then explain why the method was not sustainable.
findings.wentWrong: The calculation went well for a large share of candidates, but the explanation did not: many struggled, and answers about the method using less energy were not credited.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Multiplied the desired product's formula mass by its balancing number, added every product for the total, and then argued from the low atom economy: most of the mass wasted, raw materials used up, not cost effective.
findings.rule: Explain sustainability with atoms and money: raw materials used up, waste made, cost. Energy is a different argument and earns nothing here.

findings.asked: Calculate relative formula masses, one of them with a bracketed group.
findings.wentWrong: Mostly done well, but some candidates did not multiply the atoms inside the bracket by the number outside it, or added up the bracket wrongly.
findings.rule: Work out the bracketed group first, then multiply it by the number outside: Mg(NO₃)₂ is 24 + 2 × (14 + 48).

findings.asked: Calculate the percentage of iron in an iron(III) compound.
findings.wentWrong: Most succeeded, though a few counted iron once where the formula holds two iron atoms.
findings.rule: Every subscript multiplies the atom in front of it. Read Fe₂ as two irons before you add anything up.

insight.ruleToRemember: Convert the volume, then work in moles, one line per mark. For atom economy, multiply every formula mass by its balancing number and put the product you want over the total mass of all the products. Argue sustainability from wasted atoms and money, never energy.
insight.aStarSignal: An answer to 'why is this not sustainable' that quotes the atom economy it is arguing from, then names the raw materials used up, the waste made and the cost, in that order.
